---
title: "Differential expression"
subtitle: "Which genes respond to infection, to the TRIM28 genotype, and to both together?"
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
source("_common.R")
gene <- function(contrast, symbol_name, column) {
  deg[[contrast]][[column]][match(symbol_name, deg[[contrast]]$symbol)]
}
interaction_up_ids <- deg$interaction[direction == "up", gene_id]
n_up_induced_6kr <- sum(deg$infection_6KR[match(interaction_up_ids, gene_id), log2FC] > 0)
ora_terms <- function(q) ora_counts[query == q, `GO:BP` + KEGG + REAC]
ora_n <- function(q) ora_counts[query == q, n_genes]
ora_padj <- function(q, term) ora[query == q & term_name == term, p_adj][1]
ifn_rank <- ora[query == "infection_wt_up", which(term_name == "Interferon alpha/beta signaling")]
infection_up <- deg$infection_wt[direction == "up" & log2FC_shrunk > 1]
symbols_wt <- deg$infection_wt$symbol
is_rp <- grepl("^(RP[LS][0-9]+[AX]?|RPLP[0-2]|RPSA)$", symbols_wt)
n_rp_up <- sum(deg$infection_wt$gene_id[is_rp] %in% infection_up$gene_id)
```

## One model, five questions

All 12 samples were fitted in one DESeq2 model with the design
`~ genotype + infection + genotype:infection` and the reference levels wt and mock. The last term,
the **interaction**, asks whether infection changes a gene differently in 6KR than in wt cells.
From this single fit, five contrasts were extracted. Genes with a Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted
p-value below 0.05 count as differentially expressed.

```{r}
#| label: deg-table
contrast_text <- c(
  infection_wt = "Infected vs mock, in wt cells",
  infection_6KR = "Infected vs mock, in 6KR cells",
  genotype_mock = "6KR vs wt, in mock cells",
  genotype_infected = "6KR vs wt, in infected cells",
  interaction = "Interaction: infection effect in 6KR minus infection effect in wt"
)
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(Contrast = contrast_text[deg_counts$contrast],
             Up = n(deg_counts$up), Down = n(deg_counts$down),
             Total = n(deg_counts$significant)),
  row.names = FALSE, align = "lrrr",
  caption = sprintf("Differentially expressed genes per contrast (of %s tested genes).",
                    n(n_tested))
)
```

::: {.grid}

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-8}
**Infection changes more than half of all tested genes**, the genotype alone far fewer. Classical
interferon-stimulated genes are strongly induced in wt cells, for example OASL (shrunken log2 fold
change `r f1(gene("infection_wt", "OASL", "log2FC_shrunk"))`), whereas IFNB1 itself is not
significantly induced in wt cells at 6 hours (adjusted p =
`r signif(gene("infection_wt", "IFNB1", "padj"), 2)`), in line with the block of interferon-β
induction by the viral protein NS1.
:::

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-4}

## Explore the volcano plots

I'd say the volcano plots are the most fun part of this page, because you can play around with
them: hover over a point and you see the gene, drag to zoom in, and double-click to get back.
Each point is one gene, the x-axis shows the fold change and the y-axis how significant it is.
The fold changes are shrunk with ashr, which pulls large but noisy fold changes of weakly
expressed genes towards zero, so the plots don't get dominated by genes with only a few reads.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Infection in wt cells

```{r}
#| label: volcano-infection
plot_volcano("infection_wt", "log2 fold change, infected vs mock (shrunken)")
```

## Interaction

```{r}
#| label: volcano-interaction
plot_volcano("interaction", "interaction log2 fold change, 6KR minus wt (shrunken)")
```

## 6KR vs wt, mock cells

```{r}
#| label: volcano-genotype
plot_volcano("genotype_mock", "log2 fold change, 6KR vs wt in mock cells (shrunken)")
```

:::

## What does "interaction up" mean?

A positive interaction means that the infection effect is **higher in 6KR than in wt cells**. That
can be a stronger induction, but also a weaker repression. Of the
`r dc("interaction", "up")` interaction-up genes, `r n_up_induced_6kr` were induced by infection in
6KR cells and `r dc("interaction", "up") - n_up_induced_6kr` were repressed in wt cells and less so
in 6KR cells. The interaction-up genes include interferon-stimulated genes such as IRF1, IFIT3,
IFI16 and USP18, which fits the model of the source study: loss of SUMO-modified TRIM28
derepresses endogenous retroviruses, whose double-stranded RNA adds to the viral stimulus.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

## Which processes are affected?

Over-representation analysis with g:Profiler tested the up- and down-regulated gene lists against
GO Biological Process, KEGG and Reactome, with all tested genes as background.

![Five most significant terms per source for **a**, genes induced by infection in wt cells; **b**, interaction-up genes; **c**, genes up-regulated in mock 6KR vs wt cells. Colour gives the −log10 adjusted p-value, point size the number of list genes in the term.](assets/figures/figure_3.png){fig-alt="Dot plots of enriched terms for three gene lists" width="85%"}

- **Interaction-up genes are enriched for antiviral defence.** The
  `r ora_n("interaction_up")` interaction-up genes gave `r ora_terms("interaction_up")` terms, led by
  defence response to other organisms and to viruses and type I interferon signalling (adjusted p =
  `r signif(ora_padj("interaction_up", "defense response to virus"), 2)` for "defense response to
  virus").
- **Genotype markers point to TRIM28 function.** The `r ora_n("genotype_mock_up")` genes up in
  uninfected 6KR cells are enriched for cell adhesion, and Reactome lists "Regulation of endogenous
  retroelements by KRAB-ZFP proteins", the gene family that recruits TRIM28.
- **The infection list is led by ribosome and oxidative phosphorylation terms, not by
  interferon.** `r n_rp_up` of `r sum(is_rp)` cytosolic ribosomal protein genes are in it, while
  "Interferon alpha/beta signaling" only ranks at position `r ifn_rank`. This most likely reflects
  the virus-induced host shutoff: IAV degrades most host mRNAs, transcripts that resist it then
  appear induced after normalisation, so their increase is relative rather than absolute.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
